title: Nobody knew she had been carrying an accusation someone had made against her family.
paragraphs: Nobody knew she had been carrying an accusation someone had made against her family.
And nobody knew that while everyone was celebrating the powerful sermon, she was silently asking God a question she felt almost ashamed to pray.
“Lord, who is going to take care of us?”
Perhaps you have never been a pastor's wife.
But maybe you know what it feels like to be needed by everyone and understood by almost no one.
Maybe you know what it means to keep smiling while your own heart is breaking.
Maybe you have been praised for your strength when what you desperately needed was permission to admit you were tired.
Then stay with this story.
Because what Scripture reveals about the woman beside a shepherd may surprise you.
And what Jesus offers her is far greater than another demand to be strong.
She is a pastor's wife. But before she was ever called that, she was a daughter of God.
Somewhere along the way, many churches have forgotten the difference.
A woman marries a man who loves Jesus and believes God has called him to shepherd His people.
She dreams of building a home with him, raising children if God grants them, praying together, growing old together, and serving Christ faithfully.
Then ministry begins.
And slowly, sometimes without anyone intending it, her marriage becomes public property.
Her husband's time belongs to the congregation.
Her weekends belong to the church calendar.
Her behavior becomes a sermon people think they are entitled to evaluate.
Her clothing is examined. Her children's behavior is discussed. Her friendships are questioned. Her absence is noticed.
If she speaks boldly, someone may call her controlling.
If she remains quiet, someone may call her unfriendly.
If she serves constantly, people may assume she has endless energy.
If she rests, someone may question her commitment.
If she has a career, someone may wonder why she is not at church more often.
If she stays home, someone may underestimate the work she does.
And sometimes the most painful criticism comes from people who have never once asked how she is doing.
She learns to smile because she does not want to damage the ministry.
She learns to swallow certain words because she does not want to create conflict.
She learns to say, “We're doing well,” because explaining the truth would take more strength than she has left.
But here is something the Church must remember.
The Bible never commands a pastor's wife to become a perfect woman for public consumption.
Scripture establishes qualifications for elders and overseers, including their character, marriage, and management of their households (1 Timothy 3:1–7; Titus 1:5–9).
Those qualifications matter deeply.
Yet Scripture does not create a separate ordained office called “pastor's wife,” with an unlimited list of congregational responsibilities.

Marriage to a pastor does not automatically make a woman the church's unpaid administrator, permanent counselor, worship leader, event organizer, children's ministry director, or emotional shock absorber.
She may joyfully serve in some of these ways.
She may possess extraordinary gifts for teaching, hospitality, encouragement, administration, or mercy.
But those gifts must be recognized and exercised faithfully, not demanded simply because of the man she married.
The apostle Paul writes:
— 1 Corinthians 12:4, KJV
Different gifts.
The same Spirit.
Not every woman is called to serve in precisely the same way.
And not every pastor's wife is called to stand behind a microphone.
Some will minister publicly.
Others will serve quietly.
Some will lead women's Bible studies.
Others will disciple one person at a time.
Some will work outside the church to help provide for their families.
Others will devote significant seasons to their homes.
The measure of faithfulness is not whether she fulfills every expectation imposed upon her.
It is whether she walks faithfully with Christ in the responsibilities and opportunities He has actually given her.
And that distinction can rescue a woman from years of unnecessary guilt.
Because the congregation may have expectations.
But only Christ is Lord of her conscience.
There is another truth we need to confront.
Sometimes the loneliest woman in the church is the one everyone assumes has the strongest faith.
People hesitate to confide in her because they fear their private struggles will reach the pastor.
Others confide everything in her without considering the emotional weight of what they are sharing.
She may hear about marriages collapsing, children rebelling, church members leaving, financial difficulties, hidden sins, and painful conflicts.
She loves the people.
She wants to help.
But she is human.
And after spending an entire day absorbing other people's pain, she may return home with nothing left to give her own family.
Sometimes she wants to tell someone what she is experiencing.
Then she remembers how quickly words can travel through a congregation.
So she keeps quiet.
She cannot always tell her husband everything because he is already carrying burdens of his own.
She cannot tell the children because they are too young.
She cannot tell church members because some matters require confidentiality.
And she cannot pretend forever that silence is the same thing as spiritual maturity.
One night, perhaps, she closes the bedroom door.
She kneels beside the bed.
And the words finally come.
“Jesus, I love You. I really do. But I'm exhausted.”
That is not necessarily a prayer of rebellion.
It may be the beginning of a deeply needed moment of honesty before God.
The Psalms are filled with cries from faithful people who were frightened, overwhelmed, confused, and wounded.
David prayed:
“How long wilt thou forget me, O LORD? for ever? how long wilt thou hide thy face from me?”
— Psalm 13:1, KJV
Those words were preserved in Scripture.
God did not erase David's anguish to protect the appearance of perfect faith.
And a pastor's wife does not have to erase her anguish either.
One of the most tender invitations Jesus ever gave appears in Matthew 11:28.
“Come unto me, all ye that labour and are heavy laden, and I will give you rest.”
— Matthew 11:28, KJV
In the Greek text, Jesus addresses those described as κοπιῶντες καὶ πεφορτισμένοι (kopiōntes kai pephortismenoi).
The first word describes people laboring or growing weary through toil.
The second comes from a verb meaning to load or burden and describes people who have been weighed down.
Jesus is speaking to the weary and burdened, inviting them to find rest in Him.
We should understand the passage in its context. Jesus is not merely offering a technique for reducing stress. He is calling people to Himself, to take His yoke upon them, and to learn from Him.
He does not promise a life without responsibility.
He offers Himself as the gentle and humble Lord under whose authority weary souls can find rest.
And that matters for a pastor's wife.
Because she may have spent years believing that serving Jesus means never admitting she is tired.
But Jesus never said, “Come to Me when you have finally become strong enough.”
He said, “Come unto me.”
Not to another committee.
Not to another performance.
Not to another impossible standard.
To Him.
The Savior who calls His people to serve is also the Savior who knows they need rest.
There is a scene in Scripture that every church should remember when thinking about the families of its leaders.
Jesus had sent His apostles into demanding ministry.
They returned and reported what they had done and taught.
People were coming and going in such numbers that they did not even have leisure to eat.
And Jesus said:
“Come ye yourselves apart into a desert place, and rest a while.”
— Mark 6:31, KJV
Notice what Jesus did not say.
He did not accuse them of lacking dedication because they needed rest.
He did not suggest that exhaustion proved they were unworthy servants.
He recognized their human limitations.
The context is specifically about the apostles, not a direct command about pastoral family schedules. But the passage reveals something unmistakable about the character of Christ.
He is not indifferent to the needs of those serving Him.
So why do some churches behave as though a pastor's family must be available every hour of every day?
Why do we sometimes praise a minister for sacrificing his family while overlooking the biblical responsibility he has toward that very household?
Paul writes that an overseer must be:
— 1 Timothy 3:4, KJV
The next verse connects household leadership with caring for God's church.
A pastor's home is not an inconvenience standing in the way of ministry.
His faithfulness at home is part of the evidence of his suitability to shepherd others.
That does not mean his family must look flawless.
It means the way he loves, leads, protects, and cares for his household matters to God.
And sometimes a pastor's wife does not need another church member telling her how fortunate she is to be married to a man of God.
Sometimes she needs her husband to come home.
To put down his phone.
To listen without immediately offering a sermon.
To notice that she has been carrying more than she can bear.
To remember the woman he promised to love before the congregation ever learned his name.
Ephesians 5:25 says:
“Husbands, love your wives, even as Christ also loved the church, and gave himself for it.”
The Greek verb translated “love” is ἀγαπᾶτε (agapate), from agapaō.
In this passage, husbands are commanded to love their wives in a manner shaped by Christ's self-giving love for the Church.
It is not permission for a husband to demand endless sacrifice from his wife.
It is a command directed to the husband himself.
His love is to be sacrificial.
His leadership is not a license for selfishness.
His ministry cannot become an excuse to neglect the covenant he made before God.
A pastor cannot faithfully preach the love of Christ while treating his own wife as though her needs are insignificant.
And a congregation should never encourage that contradiction.
Because the woman beside the pastor is not merely an accessory to his calling.
She is his wife.
A person made in God's image.
A fellow heir of grace.
A sister in Christ.
And someone he is commanded to love.
There is another burden that many people rarely consider.
The pastor's wife often watches people wound the man she loves, then must decide how to love those same people.
Imagine watching your husband spend nights praying for someone.
You see him leave family meals to visit the hospital.
You watch him counsel a couple through a marriage crisis.
You know the hours he spends studying Scripture.
You see the tears he never allows the congregation to witness.
Then one Sunday, someone publicly questions his motives.
Another person spreads a rumor.
A family he has helped for years leaves the church without a conversation.
And suddenly, the man who stood behind the pulpit encouraging everyone else comes home discouraged.
His wife sees it.
She sees the silence at dinner.
She sees the sleepless nights.
She sees him wondering whether he has failed.
And perhaps her first instinct is anger.
Not because she hates the people.
But because she loves her husband.
She wants to defend him.
She wants to tell the whole story.
She wants everyone to understand what they have not seen.
But she also knows that love must not become bitterness.
And this is where following Jesus becomes painfully personal.
Paul writes:
— Ephesians 4:32, KJV
Forgiveness is not easy when the wound is fresh.
And forgiveness does not require pretending wrongdoing never happened.
It does not mean protecting abuse, covering up criminal conduct, ignoring legitimate concerns about church leadership, or refusing appropriate accountability.
Biblical forgiveness and truthful accountability are not enemies.
A pastor's wife can forgive someone while recognizing that trust must be rebuilt.
She can pray for someone while establishing necessary boundaries.
She can refuse vengeance while speaking truthfully about harm.
She can love the Church without agreeing to be mistreated by it.
And sometimes she needs to hear this clearly:
You are allowed to tell the truth about your pain without betraying Jesus.
Consider the women Scripture places before us.
Priscilla appears alongside her husband Aquila in the New Testament.
In Acts 18:26, they help Apollos understand the way of God more accurately.
Priscilla is not presented merely as a silent shadow beside her husband.
She participates in meaningful service to Christ.
But we should be careful not to force her story into a modern position the text does not explicitly assign to her. Scripture does not identify Aquila as a local church pastor in the modern sense.
What their example does show is a married couple serving the Gospel together, using their gifts to strengthen others.
Then consider Peter's household.
Mark 1:30–31 records Jesus healing Simon Peter's mother-in-law.

That passage establishes that Peter had a mother-in-law and therefore had been married. First Corinthians 9:5 also refers to the right of apostles, including Cephas, to be accompanied by a believing wife.
Yet Scripture gives us remarkably little detail about Peter's wife's personal experiences.
We should not invent a biography for her.
We do not know every sacrifice she made, every conversation she had, or every difficulty she endured.
And perhaps that silence reminds us of something important.
There are faithful people whose names and private struggles are scarcely recorded in human history.
But obscurity before people is not obscurity before God.
Hebrews 6:10 declares:
“For God is not unrighteous to forget your work and labour of love, which ye have shewed toward his name, in that ye have ministered to the saints, and do minister.”
Read those words again.
God is not unrighteous to forget.
The meal nobody thanked her for.
The visitor she welcomed when she was already exhausted.
The child she comforted after another difficult church meeting.
The quiet prayer she whispered over her husband.
The person she encouraged without ever mentioning her own struggles.
The faithful service offered from love for Christ.
God is not forgetful.
But there is an important distinction.
God's remembrance of faithful service is not a command to remain in harmful circumstances without seeking help.
She does not have to earn His love by exhausting herself.
She does not have to prove her devotion by accepting mistreatment.
She does not have to become indispensable to the church in order to matter to the Savior.
Her identity is not established by the number of ministries she manages.
It is grounded in belonging to Christ.
And that brings us to a danger that can quietly enter the heart of anyone involved in ministry.
A person can spend so much time doing things for Jesus that she begins to neglect being with Jesus.
Luke 10:38–42 tells us about Martha and Mary.
Martha was occupied with much serving.
Mary sat at Jesus' feet and listened to His word.
Martha became troubled and asked Jesus to tell Mary to help her.
Jesus answered:
“Martha, Martha, thou art careful and troubled about many things: But one thing is needful: and Mary hath chosen that good part, which shall not be taken away from her.”
— Luke 10:41–42, KJV
Jesus was not condemning all practical service.
Hospitality is good.
Serving others is good.
The problem was that Martha's anxious preoccupation had begun to eclipse what mattered most in that moment.
How many pastor's wives know that feeling?
The worship service must be prepared.
The food must be arranged.
The visitors must be welcomed.
The children must be supervised.
The women's event must be organized.
The pastor needs help.
The congregation needs attention.
And by the time everything is finished, she has spent the entire day in the house of worship without finding a quiet moment to attend to the Word of the Lord.
She may be surrounded by ministry.
Yet spiritually thirsty.
Busy with holy activities.
Yet inwardly distant.
And Jesus still speaks with tenderness.
“Martha, Martha.”
He calls her by name.
He sees her anxiety.
He redirects her attention.
Not because serving has no value.
But because communion with Him cannot be replaced by religious activity.
Dear pastor's wife, hear this.
You are not loved by Jesus because you are useful to His Church.
You are loved by grace.
And the Gospel is not a message that says, “Work harder until God finally accepts you.”
The Gospel announces what Jesus Christ has accomplished for sinners through His perfect life, atoning death, and victorious resurrection.
Ephesians 2:8–9 declares:
“For by grace are ye saved through faith; and that not of yourselves: it is the gift of God: Not of works, lest any man should boast.”
In the Greek text, the word translated “grace” is χάριτι (chariti), a form of χάρις (charis).
Here it refers to God's grace, His undeserved favor in salvation.
The passage teaches that salvation is God's gift, received through faith, not something earned through human works.
And verse 10 immediately explains that believers are created in Christ Jesus for good works.
The order matters.
We do not serve to purchase salvation.
We serve because God has graciously saved us and is transforming our lives.
This truth is essential for every Christian, including the pastor's wife.
Because if she forgets grace, ministry can become a prison of endless performance.
She may begin believing that every failure disappoints God beyond repair.
That every missed meeting makes her less faithful.
That every moment of weakness exposes her as a fraud.
That every criticism proves she is not good enough.
But the cross tells a different story.
Jesus did not die for an imaginary congregation of flawless people.
He died for sinners.
He calls people to repentance and faith.
He forgives.
He restores.
He transforms.
And His grace is not reserved for those sitting in the pews.
It is for the woman sitting beside the pastor too.
Perhaps the deepest struggle is not the criticism.
Not the schedule.
Not even the loneliness.
Perhaps it is the fear that she cannot tell anyone she is struggling because people expect her to be spiritually mature.
What happens when the pastor's wife wrestles with anxiety?
When her marriage is under strain?
When she is discouraged?
When she has questions she is afraid to voice?
When she feels resentment growing in her heart?
When she is ashamed of her own mistakes?
When she wonders whether God can still use someone as imperfect as she is?
She needs what every other believer needs.
Not a pedestal.
A Savior.
First John 1:9 says:
“If we confess our sins, he is faithful and just to forgive us our sins, and to cleanse us from all unrighteousness.”
She can repent when she has sinned.
She can receive forgiveness through Christ.
She can seek wise counsel.
She can ask for prayer.
She can acknowledge exhaustion without treating it as a moral failure.
And when her circumstances require professional counseling, medical care, or protection from harm, seeking appropriate help is not a betrayal of biblical faith.
She does not have to choose between trusting Jesus and receiving responsible care.
The Church should be a place where truth and compassion meet.
Not a place where people become experts at hiding their wounds.
There is a Hebrew word that gives us a beautiful picture of the Lord's care.
In Psalm 23:1, David writes:
יְהוָה רֹעִי לֹא אֶחְסָר
Adonai ro‘i, lo echsar.
“The LORD is my shepherd; I shall not want.”
— Psalm 23:1, KJV
The Hebrew word רֹעִי (ro‘i) means “my shepherd.”
David was not declaring that he would never face danger, grief, enemies, or hardship.
The Psalm itself speaks of the valley of the shadow of death and the presence of enemies.
His confidence was in the Lord who shepherded him through those realities.
Now consider the significance for a pastor's wife.
Her husband may be a shepherd under Christ.
But he is not her ultimate Shepherd.
The congregation may look to her husband for spiritual leadership.
But she too belongs to the care of the Lord.
Jesus identifies Himself in John 10:11:
“I am the good shepherd: the good shepherd giveth his life for the sheep.”
The Greek is:
Ἐγώ εἰμι ὁ ποιμὴν ὁ καλός.
Egō eimi ho poimēn ho kalos.
“I am the good shepherd.”
In its context, Jesus contrasts His own faithful, sacrificial care with the conduct of a hired hand who abandons the sheep when danger comes.
Christ is the Good Shepherd who lays down His life for His sheep.
And the pastor's wife is one of His sheep.
She does not exist merely to help shepherd everyone else.
She needs to be shepherded by Christ.
She needs His Word.
His mercy.
His correction.
His comfort.
His grace.
His truth.
And she needs a church community willing to care for her as a fellow believer rather than treating her as an endless source of spiritual labor.
Imagine what would happen if churches remembered that.
Imagine a congregation that stopped expecting the pastor's wife to attend every event.
Imagine members who encouraged her to use her actual gifts rather than assigning her a role she never accepted.
Imagine leaders who protected the pastor's family from unreasonable demands.
Imagine mature women who offered genuine friendship without gossip or hidden agendas.
Imagine people who prayed for her without demanding access to her private life.
Imagine church members who respected her children's privacy and did not expect them to perform holiness for public approval.
Imagine a congregation where concerns about leadership could be raised responsibly, fairly, and biblically, without slander or intimidation.
Imagine a church where the pastor's wife could say, “I need help,” and hear, “We love you. How can we support you?”
That would not weaken the ministry.
It could strengthen the health and integrity of the entire church.
Galatians 6:2 says:
“Bear ye one another's burdens, and so fulfil the law of Christ.”
Notice the words.
One another.
Not everyone placing their burdens on one exhausted woman.
Not the pastor's family carrying every problem while the congregation watches.
The Christian community is called to mutual care.
And pastors' families are not excluded from that command.
Perhaps you are reading this as a church member.
You love your pastor.
You appreciate his preaching.
You are grateful for the sacrifices he makes.
Then remember the people waiting for him when the church doors close.
Pray for his marriage.
Respect his family's time.
Be considerate about unnecessary late-night calls.
Do not use his wife as a shortcut to reach him.
Do not assume she knows everything happening in the church.
Do not place your expectations on her children.
And when you see her, consider asking a question that does not require her to solve another problem.
“How are you really doing?”
Then be willing to listen.
Not to gather information.
Not to satisfy curiosity.
But to love your sister in Christ.
And perhaps you are a pastor reading this.
Your wife may be more tired than you realize.
She may love the ministry while grieving what it has cost your family.
She may be proud of your calling while wishing she had more of your attention.
She may have stood beside you through battles that few people will ever understand.
Do not assume her silence means everything is fine.
Ask her.
Listen carefully.
Give her room to be honest without becoming defensive.
Remember that a healthy marriage requires more than sharing a ministry calendar.
It requires love, attention, repentance, forgiveness, faithfulness, and time.
You may preach to hundreds.
But you are also called to love the woman you married.
And if there have been seasons when ministry has become an excuse for neglect, the path forward is not another polished explanation.
It is humble repentance followed by meaningful change.
The same Gospel you proclaim from the pulpit must shape the way you live at home.
Now, to the pastor's wife who has quietly carried more than anyone knows.
You do not have to become everything to everyone.
You cannot save the congregation.
You cannot control every opinion.
You cannot prevent every misunderstanding.
You cannot repair every broken relationship.
You cannot guarantee that every person who enters the church will remain.
You cannot carry your husband's calling in his place.
And you cannot be the Holy Spirit for the people around you.
Those responsibilities were never yours.
Christ is the Savior.
Christ is the Head of the Church.
Christ is the Good Shepherd.
Christ is the One who builds His Church.
You are called to follow Him faithfully, not to replace Him.
There will be seasons of joy.
Seasons when you see lives transformed by the Gospel.
Seasons when a marriage is restored, a wandering believer returns, a new Christian is baptized, or a struggling family finds hope.
There will be moments when you look across the sanctuary and realize that God has allowed you to witness something beautiful.
And there may be seasons of sorrow.
Seasons when people leave.
When plans fail.
When finances become difficult.
When criticism hurts.
When the children need more attention.
When your marriage requires serious work.
When you need to step back from responsibilities that have become unhealthy.
Both kinds of seasons can become occasions to trust Christ.
But neither determines your worth before Him.
Your worth is not measured by the size of your husband's congregation.
Not by the number of people who praise you.
Not by how often your family appears on social media.
Not by whether everyone approves of your decisions.
Not by whether you have mastered the art of smiling through pain.
You belong to Jesus Christ.
And no church title can make that identity greater.
There is one more picture I want you to hold in your heart.
Return to that empty sanctuary.
The pastor's wife is still sitting in the second row.
The lights are dim.
The room that was filled with worship is quiet again.
She has been trying to find the words to pray.
Finally, she whispers:
“Lord, I don't know how to keep doing everything.”
And perhaps, as she opens her Bible, her eyes fall upon 2 Corinthians 12:9.
“My grace is sufficient for thee: for my strength is made perfect in weakness.”
These were the Lord's words to Paul in the context of his plea concerning the thorn in his flesh.
They were not a promise that every painful circumstance would immediately disappear.
They were an assurance that Christ's grace was sufficient even when the weakness remained.
And that is a truth she can hold.
Not because she will never need help.
Not because she should continue carrying unhealthy burdens.
Not because her pain is insignificant.
But because the strength of Christ is not limited by the weakness of His people.
She does not need to manufacture a flawless life to prove that Jesus is faithful.
She can acknowledge her limitations.
She can confess her sins.
She can seek help.
She can make wise changes.
She can forgive.
She can establish boundaries.
She can love her husband without idolizing him.
She can serve the Church without becoming enslaved to its expectations.
And she can trust that the Savior who redeemed her is still at work in her.
This is where our theme becomes more than a beautiful phrase.
Because sometimes the scandal is not a public moral failure.
Sometimes it is the quiet contradiction of a church that preaches love while overlooking the suffering of its own people.
Sometimes it is a marriage that appears strong in public while privately needing repentance, reconciliation, and healing.
Sometimes it is the discovery that the woman everyone thought was spiritually invincible is simply a human being in desperate need of grace.
And sometimes the scandal is our own pride, resentment, bitterness, hypocrisy, or refusal to admit that we need the mercy we so readily preach to others.
But grace does not mean pretending sin is harmless.
Grace calls us to the cross.
To repentance.
To forgiveness through Jesus Christ.
To truth.
To restoration where restoration is possible.
To transformation by the Holy Spirit.
The Gospel does not merely improve our public image.
It confronts our sin and offers us a new life in Christ.
That is why Jesus rewrites everything.
Not by denying what happened.
Not by excusing wrongdoing.
Not by guaranteeing that every relationship will be restored exactly as it was.
But by redeeming sinners, transforming hearts, and giving hope that rests in His finished work rather than our ability to maintain appearances.
And that is a message worth bringing into every church.
If you are a pastor's wife, please hear this before you close this article.
You are not forgotten.
Your tears are not beneath God's attention.
Your spiritual health matters.
Your marriage matters.
Your children matter.
Your need for rest matters.
Your faithfulness matters.
And most of all, the Lord Jesus Christ is worthy of your trust.
You are not required to be everyone's savior.
You already have one.
If this article has touched a wound you rarely speak about, I want to invite you into an honest conversation.
You do not have to reveal private details to be prayed for.
Not merely to increase its reach, but because somewhere in your circle there may be a pastor's wife who has been silently wondering whether anyone understands.
Someone may need these words today.

Invite your family, friends, struggling believers, seekers, and even those who have grown distant from the faith to follow along. The truth of Jesus Christ is not reserved for people who already have everything together.
It is good news for sinners who need a Savior.
And if this message has strengthened you, I want to invite you to help us carry more Christ-centered teaching to more people.
Gospel Warrior exists to point people toward Jesus Christ through biblical truth, repentance, grace, discipleship, encouragement, and spiritual growth.
We want these resources to keep reaching people who are hungry for the Word of God, including those who may not have the financial means to purchase Christian learning materials.
You glorify Him through faith in Christ, obedience to His Word, love for others, and a life shaped by His grace.
These items can serve as reminders of biblical truth, gifts of encouragement, and opportunities to share your faith.
But the heart of the invitation is not merchandise.
It is helping people encounter the Word of God.
It is making Christ-centered encouragement and resources more accessible.
It is continuing to proclaim that broken people can find forgiveness, redemption, and new life through Jesus Christ.
Pray for this ministry.
Point a struggling friend toward the free library.
Encourage a pastor's wife.
Support your local church faithfully.
And above everything else, keep pointing people to Jesus.
Only Jesus saves.
Only His blood atones for sin.
Only His resurrection secures our living hope.
And only His grace can transform a life from the inside out.
So tonight, if you know a pastor's wife, pray for her.
If you are married to one, cherish her.
If you are part of her congregation, love her as your sister in Christ.
And if you are that woman, sitting quietly in a sanctuary after everyone else has gone home, remember this:
The church may know you as the pastor's wife, but Jesus knows you by name—and when everyone else has gone home, your Shepherd has not abandoned you.
